  "39395114": {
    "kind": "consensus",
    "limitations": [
      "The recommendations preferring RLT over targeted agents and over chemotherapy rest on cross-trial comparison and retrospective series rather than head-to-head data, which the panel reflects in grades of 2b - B and 3b - A, and it notes that COMPETE and COMPOSE are still running.",
      "The G2-G3 recommendation is written in anticipation of a regulatory approval that had not yet occurred, hence the phrasing 'once approved'.",
      "The frail-patient recommendation is graded level 5, that is expert opinion, and rests on a single retrospective matched cohort.",
      "The literature search was deliberately restricted to 177Lu-DOTATATE, so the document cannot speak to 90Y-DOTATOC or newer radioligands, nor to the intra-arterial and combination strategies it mentions.",
      "The panel sets out the limits of RECIST 1.1 in this disease at length: these tumours may stabilise or even enlarge while responding, central necrosis during RLT produces false-positive size increases, and shrinkage can be delayed, so RECIST should be applied cautiously in slow-growing GEP-NET.",
      "The Choi criteria perform equally or markedly better in published comparisons but rely on portal venous phase images while arterial phase is standard for these vascular tumours, which the panel calls a major limitation on using Choi in the neuroendocrine context.",
      "Chemotherapy is retained as the choice for pancreatic NET with high tumour burden, tumour-related symptoms or rapid progression, a carve-out from the panel's own recommendation to prefer RLT."
    ],
    "critique": [
      "The grading does not track the evidence. The recommendation to prefer radioligand therapy over chemotherapy is given the document's strongest recommendation grade (A) on one of its weakest evidence levels (3b), while the recommendation to prefer it over everolimus or sunitinib carries better evidence (2b) and a weaker grade (B). A reader cannot tell what the letters mean.",
      "The central second-line recommendation is built from a 508-patient matched retrospective series (progression-free survival 2.2 against 0.6 years) and a phase 2 trial in pancreatic NET (OCLURANDOM, 12-month progression-free survival 80.5% against 42%). No randomised head-to-head comparison of radioligand therapy against everolimus, sunitinib or chemotherapy existed when this was written, and the document's own grades concede it.",
      "Early incorporation of radioligand therapy is recommended at the document's highest level, 1b - A, on the reasoning that high tumour burden reduces its efficacy. That is a prognostic observation. No trial randomised early against delayed radioligand therapy, so the strength of this recommendation is not supported by the kind of evidence a 1b label implies.",
      "Pre-committing to a recommendation 'once approved' leaves practice tied to a regulatory decision, and the trial behind it does not match the recommendation's scope. NETTER-2 enrolled newly diagnosed patients with no documented progression, required uptake score 3 or 4 in every target lesion, capped Ki-67 at 55% and excluded anyone with prior hepatic embolisation or ablation, none of which qualifies the statement here.",
      "There is no surgical or liver-directed content whatever. Locoregional therapy appears only as something to be excluded on pre-RLT imaging, and the document says nothing about debulking, embolisation, radioembolisation or sequencing in liver-dominant disease, although hepatic tumour burden is the very variable it invokes to argue for treating early.",
      "The retreatment recommendation rests on a confounded observation. Patients who reached a cumulative renal absorbed dose of 23 Gy had nearly double the median progression-free and overall survival, but reaching a higher cumulative dose requires surviving and tolerating more cycles, so the association is in part a consequence of doing well rather than a cause of it.",
      "Dosimetry is invoked to tailor the retreatment dose and no dosimetry protocol, renal constraint beyond the 23 Gy figure, or marrow constraint is specified anywhere.",
      "The method is thin for a document of this reach. Ten questions, a MEDLINE search whose dates and search strings are not reported in the body, grades assigned by the panel itself, and no independent evidence review, no external review and no voting or agreement statistic described.",
      "A level 5 recommendation, that is pure expert opinion, is given strength B for treating frail patients, a combination the grading framework the panel invokes does not support.",
      "Seven named authors declare consultancy or speaker honoraria from Advanced Accelerator Applications, Novartis, ITM, Ipsen, Recordati, Advanz, Harpoon Therapeutics, Merck or Harbour Biomedical, and the document's single most consequential output is a recommendation to prefer those companies' radioligand over competing drug classes.",
      "A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment, so a set of recommendations that reorders second-line therapy for this disease entered the literature without external appraisal."
    ],
    "n": "No patient cohort. A four-society Italian panel answered ten predefined questions from a MEDLINE search restricted to 177Lu-DOTATATE plus expert opinion, assigning each statement a level of evidence (1 to 5) and a strength of recommendation (A to D).",
    "bottom_line": "This four-society Italian consensus moves radioligand therapy to second line in somatostatin-receptor-positive gastroenteropancreatic NET, ahead of high-dose somatostatin analogue, everolimus, sunitinib and chemotherapy, and recommends incorporating it early on the grounds that high tumour burden reduces its efficacy. Only the comparison with high-dose somatostatin analogue rests on randomised evidence; preference over targeted agents comes from one phase 2 trial and preference over chemotherapy from a matched retrospective series, which the panel itself grades 2b and 3b while attaching strength A to the weaker of the two. The document is silent on surgery and liver-directed therapy, mentioning locoregional treatment only as something to exclude on pre-treatment imaging, so it cannot be used to decide between radioligand therapy and debulking or embolisation in liver-dominant disease.",
    "funding": "Open access funding provided by Universita degli Studi di Roma La Sapienza within the CRUI-CARE Agreement; no study funding is declared. Seven named authors declare consultancy or speaker honoraria outside the submitted work from Advanced Accelerator Applications, Novartis, ITM, Ipsen, Recordati, Advanz, Harpoon Therapeutics, Merck and Harbour Biomedical; the remaining authors declare no conflict of interest."
  },
  "40302310": {
    "kind": "cohort",
    "limitations": [
      "A prospectively collected trial cohort is compared with a retrospective PRRT-only cohort.",
      "The PRRT-only cohort suffered from reporting bias, which forced the authors to drop the toxicity analysis and the analysis of hormone-related complaints altogether.",
      "Heterogeneity of the primary tumours made propensity-score matching difficult and limited it to 1:1, and even with restrictive inclusion and matching criteria an imbalance in ECOG score remained.",
      "No patient in the combination cohort had received prior chemotherapy against 21% of the PRRT-only cohort, an imbalance that could not be entered into the propensity model.",
      "The finding that every combination-cohort patient rose at least one ECOG point after PRRT is described as striking, and the authors caution that it may reflect less rigorous retrospective data collection rather than a real difference.",
      "Too few patients had liver-only disease to run the separate analysis that would most support the hypothesis, so no solid evidence is offered for the population the authors think would benefit most.",
      "The gastrointestinal versus pancreatic subgroup difference rests on very small numbers and the authors say it warrants confirmation.",
      "There is no clear definition of liver-dominant disease in the literature or in any guideline, which the authors identify as a basic obstacle to positioning SIRT at all.",
      "Concerns about long-term hepatotoxicity rest on small retrospective studies describing pseudo-cirrhotic imaging morphology whose clinical implications remain unknown.",
      "Short-term quality of life is not hampered by SIRT but long-term quality-of-life effects remain unknown, and no quality-of-life data were collected here.",
      "All available SIRT data in NET, including this study, use a one-size-fits-all fixed activity; the authors state that personalised dosimetry is now standard elsewhere and that prospective dosimetry studies are needed."
    ],
    "critique": [
      "The primary endpoint is reported as two proportions with heavily overlapping confidence intervals and no between-group test at all: 68% (95% CI 43-87) against 55% (32-76). No hazard ratio and no p value is given for the primary comparison, and the same is true of the hepatic PFS figures (82%, 57-96 against 50%, 28-72) on which the conclusion actually rests.",
      "After matching, the arm receiving the extra liver-directed treatment had less liver disease, not more. Median liver tumour burden was 8% in the combination cohort against 20% in the PRRT-only cohort (6% against 13% at the 3-month scan), even though fractional liver involvement at 3 months was one of the ten covariates in the final propensity model, and even though the whole rationale of the study is bulky hepatic disease.",
      "Both arms are given a guaranteed event-free run-in. Patients who progressed by RECIST at the 3-month scan after the last PRRT cycle were removed, while progression-free survival is measured from the first PRRT cycle, so roughly nine months of PRRT plus three months of restaging are credited to every patient before an event can be recorded.",
      "How many patients that exclusion removed from each matched arm cannot be worked out. The text gives 4 (13%) in the combination cohort and 16 (18%) in the PRRT-only cohort and cites Table 2, which presents the matched sets of 24, yet 16 of 24 would be 67%; the percentages belong to the full analysis sets and the matched-set figures are never stated.",
      "The ECOG imbalance the authors could not match on is the strongest evidence that the two cohorts were observed differently rather than being clinically different. Performance status was balanced before PRRT and then diverged completely afterwards, with 0% of the combination cohort and 75% of the controls at ECOG 0, which is what prospective trial monitoring against retrospective chart abstraction would produce. The paper acknowledges the possibility and then uses the same observation to argue that its treated cohort was the sicker one.",
      "The argument that the combination cohort had worse prognosis is assembled selectively. More pulmonary metastases are cited as adverse, fewer bone metastases are noted as pointing the other way, extrahepatic disease differed in the full analysis set (83% versus 64%) but was balanced after matching (88% in both), and less liver disease is not mentioned in that passage at all.",
      "Matching discards most of the control pool. Ninety PRRT-only patients were collected and 24 used, with a ten-covariate logistic propensity model fitted across 120 patients to produce those pairs, and no overlap or common-support diagnostics are reported beyond a balance figure.",
      "The combination cohort is defined by having completed and tolerated four full cycles of PRRT and then being fit enough for radioembolisation within 20 weeks. Being alive, non-progressing and well enough for a second procedure is an eligibility requirement in one arm and not the other, however carefully the controls are matched on baseline covariates.",
      "The subgroup numbers do not agree between the results and the discussion. The gastrointestinal and pancreatic subgroups are given as n=10 versus 14 and n=6 versus 7 in the results, and as n=13 versus 15 and n=8 versus 7 in the discussion, for the single finding the paper describes as most interesting.",
      "The benefit is hepatic and the endpoints that matter clinically are unchanged. Median PFS was 30.8 against 30.3 months and median hepatic PFS 33.5 against 30.3 months, with no overall survival difference, so the case for adding SIRT rests entirely on two-year landmark proportions and on a response rate measured in the organ that was irradiated.",
      "Best objective response is the softest available endpoint for this comparison. Radioembolisation produces necrosis and cavitation in treated lesions, and a 71% versus 25% response rate measured by RECIST size change in an irradiated liver cannot be separated from the direct physical effect of the treatment on the target lesions.",
      "No dosimetry of any kind is reported: no absorbed dose to tumour or to normal liver, no dose-volume metrics, in a study of two sequential radiation treatments to the same organ. The authors raise the point themselves as a general deficiency of the field, having run their own study the same way.",
      "The two analyses a clinician would most want, toxicity and hormonal symptom control, were abandoned because the retrospective arm's records would not support them. A combination of two radiation therapies is therefore recommended as safe and feasible on the basis of a comparison in which safety could not be compared.",
      "The funder manufactures the product. The study is funded by Terumo, which makes the holmium-166 microspheres, two co-authors are employed by Medical Affairs Interventional Oncology at Terumo Europe NV and a third is from a commercial biostatistics company, and the conflict-of-interest statement reads that the authors declare no conflicts of interest.",
      "A PubMed search found no linked editorial or comment, so this propensity-matched comparison of a single-arm trial against a historical cohort entered the literature without independent appraisal."
    ],
    "n": "24 matched pairs: the 30 patients of the prospective single-arm HEPAR PLuS phase 2 trial set against 90 PRRT-only patients collected retrospectively from four European ENETS Centres of Excellence, reduced to 1:1 matching on a ten-covariate propensity score.",
    "bottom_line": "This suggests that adding holmium-166 radioembolisation after four cycles of 177Lu-DOTATATE improves control of liver disease, with two-year hepatic progression-free survival of 82% against 50% and an intrahepatic response rate of 75% against 29% in 24 matched pairs. It does not establish benefit: the primary endpoint is two proportions with overlapping confidence intervals and no statistical test, median PFS and overall survival are unchanged, the combination arm had less liver disease after matching (8% against 20% burden) despite bulky disease being the rationale, and toxicity could not be compared at all. The one arm is a prospective trial cohort that had to survive and tolerate full PRRT to qualify, the other a retrospective chart series, and the study is funded by the microsphere manufacturer with two of its employees as co-authors under a declaration of no conflicts.",
    "funding": "Funded by Terumo, the manufacturer of the holmium-166 microspheres studied. Two co-authors are employed by Medical Affairs Interventional Oncology, Terumo Europe NV, Leuven, and one is from Barton Biostatistics Ltd; the paper nonetheless states that the authors declare no conflicts of interest."
  }

    "bottom_line": "Establishes that transplantation can give 75 percent four-year survival and 83 percent recurrence-free survival in cirrhotic patients with a single HCC of 5 cm or less or up to three nodules of 3 cm or less, and that tumours exceeding those limits do much worse. It does not validate the limits as a selection rule, because they were applied to explant pathology in the same 48 patients that generated them, with only four recurrences, no external cohort, and no analysis from the point of listing.",
    "funding": "Supported by the Italian Association for Cancer Research; no conflict-of-interest statement appears anywhere in the article, and the acknowledgements thank staff of Sandoz, Fujisawa and Knoll"
  },
  "8831597": {
    "kind": "cohort",
    "limitations": [
      "Unresolved decompensation was intentionally screened for, which the authors say probably explains their 38 percent rate against the lower figures in retrospective series",
      "Hepatic vein catheterisation is not performed routinely in most centres, as the authors concede, and the non-invasive alternatives they examined were significant only on univariate analysis",
      "The authors cannot explain why a lower blood urea nitrogen was associated with decompensation and note that the values stayed within the normal range",
      "The authors note that mean bilirubin was within the normal range in both groups, so a normal bilirubin does not rule out the risk of postoperative decompensation",
      "The authors state that their recommendation rests on patients selected by the best available criteria at one centre in one era, and defend the result against alternative explanations by reference to their own concurrent surgical series"
    ],
    "critique": [
      "Forty-four clinical, laboratory, tumour and haemodynamic parameters were screened univariably and six carried into a logistic regression fitted to 11 events, so the model is overfitted by any standard and the odds ratio of 1.90 per mmHg (95% CI 1.12 to 3.22) is not a stable estimate",
      "The dichotomy is perfectly separating (11 of 15 versus 0 of 14), and a logistic regression containing a near-perfectly separating covariate does not produce trustworthy coefficients or p values; the reported P = 0.0001 for the multivariable term is no stronger than the univariable comparison it repeats",
      "No derivation of the 10 mmHg threshold is described: no cut-point search, no receiver-operating analysis and no alternative thresholds are reported, because 10 mmHg is the conventional definition of clinically significant portal hypertension carried over from the variceal literature and applied here after the fact",
      "The cohort mean gradient was 9.9 plus or minus 4.4 mmHg, so the cut-point sits almost exactly at the mean of a narrow continuous distribution, which is the split that maximises apparent separation and the one least likely to reproduce",
      "The endpoint is not liver failure: 16 of the 17 early events were ascites, all 11 unresolved events had ascites requiring diuretics with one jaundice and one encephalopathy, and the single death was septic shock with multiorgan failure, so the guideline-shaping outcome is diuretic-requiring ascites at 3 months",
      "Ascites management was protocolised (40 mEq sodium, furosemide and spironolactone as needed) by the same unblinded team that had measured the gradient, so the endpoint of requiring diuretics is partly a treatment decision by clinicians who knew the exposure",
      "The paper reports no survival outcome of any kind, yet its recommendation is that resection be restricted; recurrence was in fact numerically more common in the group without decompensation (9 versus 4), and the claim that decompensation shortens survival is supported only by the authors' own prior abstract",
      "No postoperative haemodynamic measurement was made in any patient, so the mechanism offered, unchanged portal inflow through a reduced non-compliant vascular bed, is imported from a rat model and never tested in this cohort",
      "The authors conclude that surgical factors cannot explain the findings because resection type, ischaemia time and transfusion did not differ, but those comparisons are made between 11 and 18 patients and have essentially no power to exclude a surgical effect",
      "Two of the six univariable predictors point in directions the authors cannot account for, a lower blood urea nitrogen and a bilirubin difference within the normal range, which is what fitting six variables to 11 events in 29 patients produces",
      "The gradient was measured once, in the right hepatic vein, within 10 days of surgery, with no repeat measurement, no reproducibility estimate and no interobserver data, in a study where the clinical decision turns on a few mmHg either side of the cut-point",
      "Follow-up for the endpoint stops at 3 months and no longer-term liver or oncological outcome is reported, so the paper cannot show that the patients it would exclude from resection do better with any alternative",
      "The Discussion's proposed algorithm ends by recommending percutaneous ethanol injection as potentially radical only in tumours larger than 3 cm, the opposite of the finding in the reference it cites for that claim, which reported that efficacy falls with increasing tumour size",
      "No conflict-of-interest statement appears, and the same group went on to embed this single-centre threshold in the BCLC staging system and in the EASL and AASLD recommendations it now underwrites"

The separation is perfect in a cohort of 29 with 11 events screened against 44 candidate variables, the 10 mmHg line was imported rather than derived here, the endpoint is almost entirely diuretic-requiring ascites, and no survival outcome is reported at all.",
    "funding": "Supported in part by grants from the Fondo de Investigaciones Sanitarias (FIS 93/0544 and 94/0757) and the Direccion General de Investigacion Cientifica y Tecnica (DGICYT PB94-1562); no conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article"
  },
  "39802807": {
    "kind": "rct",
    "n": "236 treated patients with HCC ≤4 cm in the device-specific MWA versus single-needle RFA trial.",
    "limitations": [

    ],
    "critique": [

    ],
    "bottom_line": "Sugimoto 2025: 2-year lesion-level local progression was 20/122 (16.4%) with MWA versus 38/125 (30.4%) with single-needle RFA; RR 0.54 (95% CI 0.33–0.87), P=.007. No overall-survival advantage was demonstrated."
  }
}

    "25014687": {
      "label": "CLARINET",
      "design": "RCT",
      "arms": "Lanreotide vs placebo",
      "result": "Primary endpoint met: median PFS not reached vs 18.0 mo (HR 0.47, 95% CI 0.30-0.73); 24-mo PFS 65.1% vs 33.0%; no OS or QoL difference",
      "caution": "96% stable; grade 2 HR 0.45 (0.22–0.91), pancreatic HR 0.58 (0.32–1.04); no predictive cutoff",
      "quotes": [
        "204 patients with unresectable or metastatic, somatostatin-receptor-positive, grade 1 or 2 (Ki-67 under 10%) non-functioning enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours randomised at 48 centres in 14 countries between June 2006 and April 2013: 101 to lanreotide Autogel 120 mg and 103 to placebo, with 96% having had no documented progression in the preceding 3 to 6 months.",
        "CLARINET establishes that lanreotide 120 mg delays radiographic progression in somatostatin-receptor-positive, grade 1 or 2 enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, with a hazard ratio of 0.47 and 65% versus 33% progression-free at 24 months, and it does so across hepatic tumour volumes above and below 25%. What it does not establish is that this changes anything a patient feels or how long they live: no statistically significant difference in overall survival or quality of life was demonstrated, the population was non-functioning and 96% radiographically stable at entry, and subgroup estimates do not establish a predictive grade threshold; grade 2 HR was 0.45 (95% CI 0.22–0.91). The placebo arm ran a median 18.0 months without progression, which is the figure to carry into any discussion of whether to start treatment now or watch, and the hepatic-volume subgroup everyone quotes was collapsed from five prespecified categories to two after the data were in.",
        "The subgroup that matters most for liver-directed decisions is a post hoc construction. Hepatic tumour volume was prespecified in five categories whose estimated hazard ratios ranged from 0.24 to 0.54, and was collapsed after the fact into a dichotomy at 25%. The conclusion that the effect holds irrespective of hepatic tumour volume rests on that simplification, as the paper's own table footnote states.",
        "CLARINET’s grade 2 subgroup HR was 0.45 (95% CI 0.22–0.91). The HR 0.58 (0.32–1.04) belongs to the pancreatic-primary subgroup. Subgroup estimates do not establish differential benefit by grade or primary site.",
        "CLARINET subgroup estimates are exploratory: the pancreatic subgroup HR was 0.58 (95% CI 0.32–1.04), hepatic tumour volume >25% HR 0.45 (0.23–0.88), and grade 2 HR 0.45 (0.22–0.91). These are different strata. The estimates do not establish a predictive primary-site, grade or liver-volume cutoff.",
        "The whole benefit is radiographic. Overall survival did not differ, EORTC QLQ-C30 global health status did not differ, and the population was non-functioning by design so there were no hormonal symptoms to improve. Crossover is invoked to explain the survival null without any crossover numbers or a sensitivity analysis being presented.",
        "The size of the effect is unknown because the trial ended before it could be measured. Median progression-free survival was not reached with lanreotide within the 96-week fixed study duration, so the delay is known only to exceed the observation window, and the 96-week design cannot address how long treatment should continue.",
        "Progression-free survival and time to tumour progression return the identical 18.0-month placebo median from different event counts (60 against 58), which shows the median sits in a sparse region of the curve where two events make no difference to the estimate.",
        "The chromogranin A result is reported on 64 of 101 and 64 of 103 patients, roughly two-thirds of each arm, with no account of the missing third, and it is a biochemical change in a non-functioning tumour population where it carries no symptomatic meaning.",
        "Enrolment required somatostatin-receptor scintigraphy uptake of grade 2 or higher within the previous 6 months, so the trial selected the patients most likely to respond and says nothing about receptor-poor disease, which is precisely the group in whom embolisation, chemotherapy or resection is being weighed.",
        "The trial excluded any prior radionuclide therapy at any time, chemoembolisation or chemotherapy within 6 months, and more than 15 days of previous somatostatin analogue. The cohort is therefore essentially naive to liver-directed treatment, and nothing in the result informs sequencing with embolisation, radioembolisation or PRRT.",
        "The discussion raises the obvious reading of its own data, that an 18-month placebo median supports watchful waiting, and sets it aside on the ground that the study examined prevention of progression. That is a restatement of the trial's design, not an answer to the question of whether delaying treatment costs the patient anything.",
        "The adverse events that matter for a surgical population are presented as reassurance. Cholelithiasis occurred in 10% against 3% and hyperglycaemia in 5% against 0%, and the serious treatment-related events in the lanreotide arm include biliary fistula and cholelithiasis, in patients who may later need hepatectomy or arterial therapy; the discussion calls the safety profile favourable by comparison with targeted agents and chemotherapy.",
        "The sponsor controlled the trial end to end. Ipsen, which markets lanreotide, designed, funded and conducted the study; the contract research organisation's statisticians worked under the oversight of the sponsor's own biostatistics department; a medical writer paid by the sponsor drafted the manuscript; and one co-author is affiliated to Ipsen.",
        "Two letters in the New England Journal of Medicine with an author reply are linked to this paper in PubMed (PMIDs 25317882, 25317883 and 25317881). The full texts could not be obtained, so no point above draws on them and whatever objections they raise are not represented here."
      ]

'reference_groups' and 'reference_links': explicit, reviewed presentation of source-study evidence from the HCC treatment references (liver-directed reference, systemic matrix, HCC roadmap text and critique records) for the linked modality or regimen, with the studied population, treatment arms and endpoint/horizon; every number is guarded against that study's verified site text or an exact quoted passage. {
  "key": "icca",
  "short": "iCCA",
  "name": "Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma",
  "version": "v0.8",
  "batch": "Batch 09, 15 October 2026",
  "lead": "Confirm the diagnosis, describe the number and distribution of liver tumors, stage the disease, and assess resection, systemic treatment, liver-directed therapy, and protocol-based transplantation.",
  "gatelabel": "Clinical decisions",
  "gates": [
    {
      "id": "1",
      "tone": "cure",
      "name": "1 · Confirm diagnosis and stage disease",
      "req": "all",
      "crit": [
        "Histology consistent with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, or a high-suspicion mass accepted for direct resection after multidisciplinary HPB review",
        "Multiphase CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis plus liver MRI with cholangiographic (MRCP) sequences, completed before any stent is placed",
        "Another primary excluded — colonoscopy, age-appropriate breast imaging and a CK7/CK20/CDX2-type panel as indicated",
        "Perihilar and distal cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancer require their own treatment assessment. Mixed HCC-iCCA has a separate combined-tumor roadmap; NLRB transplant guidance groups it with iCCA (see clinical decision 10).",
        "Recorded: tumour number and size, vascular and biliary involvement, nodal status, extrahepatic sites, ECOG, Child-Pugh and bilirubin, CA 19-9 and CEA, hepatitis serology"
      ],
      "ask": "Is the diagnosis established, and have all liver lesions, lymph nodes, and distant sites been assessed?",
      "standard": [
        {
          "t": "There is no imaging-only diagnosis of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma: unlike hepatocellular carcinoma, where LR-5 imaging in an at-risk population is diagnostic, histologic confirmation is required before systemic therapy or a tissue-defined transplant assessment; selected clearly resectable masses may proceed directly to surgery after multidisciplinary review.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "B",
          "refs": [
            "nccn",
            "36083140",
            "37770126",
            "37084797",
            "mhroadmap"
          ],
          "pref": "Every patient whose next step is systemic therapy, trial entry or tissue-defined transplant assessment — in those destinations the tissue criteria are not optional, and transplant assessment additionally needs the biopsy to grade differentiation and to exclude a mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma.",
          "avoid": "Do not demand a core from a high-suspicion, clearly resectable mass as a universal rule. NCCN states a suspicious mass on imaging in the proper clinical setting should be treated as malignant, and multidisciplinary HPB review may permit direct resection; the roadmap replaces universal pre-treatment biopsy with destination-specific confirmation.",
          "note": "AASLD 2023 and BSG 2023 require histological confirmation and LCSGJ 2022 regards biopsy as basically unnecessary for a typical resectable mass, so whether a core stays mandatory before resection is a local approval item (alignment worksheet, area 1). CEA and CA 19-9 are baseline and monitoring tests and never establish the diagnosis; CA 19-9 rises with biliary obstruction or cholangitis, so record it alongside the bilirubin and repeat it once the obstruction is relieved."
        },
        {
          "t": "Complete staging and biliary imaging before non-emergency instrumentation. Measure the future liver remnant when major hepatectomy is being considered.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "B",
          "refs": [
            "nccn",
            "37770126",
            "37084797"
          ],
          "pref": "Any patient with a tumour obstructing the biliary tree who might be resected — reactive change from a stent obscures ductal extent, which is exactly what decides whether biliary resection and reconstruction are needed. MRI is the study that characterises the biliary and vascular relationships that determine resectability, and EASL-ILCA prefers it over CT for intrahepatic staging.",
          "avoid": "Do not wait for imaging in cholangitis — that is drained without waiting for the discussion, and urgent sepsis treatment takes priority over the elective sequence.",
          "note": "Where the tumour obstructs the biliary tree, the need for drainage, its route and its side are decided with the hepatobiliary surgeon before any non-emergency procedure; resection without preoperative drainage can be considered when the future remnant is large. That drainage rule is grade D on its own — no comparative outcome data in intrahepatic disease were identified for it — while the grade B on this string covers the imaging sequence, which BSG 2023 and EASL-ILCA both recommend."
        },
        {
          "t": "Exclude another primary before committing to this pathway, because metastatic adenocarcinoma can be histologically indistinguishable from intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "D",
          "refs": [
            "mhroadmap"
          ],
          "pref": "Any adenocarcinoma in the liver without an established primary, and particularly before a patient is started on a biliary-tract regimen or entered into a biliary trial.",
          "avoid": "Do not let the immunohistochemical panel consume the whole core: BSG 2023 asks that tissue be reserved for molecular profiling when immunohistochemistry is planned, and whether to add that instruction is a local approval item (alignment worksheet, area 12).",
          "note": "Treating a colorectal or pancreatic metastasis as intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is a recognised and consequential error. Hepatitis B and C status and any cirrhosis are established at entry: they change operative risk and, where a mixed tumour is possible, the differential."
        },
        {
          "t": "Describe every suspected tumor nodule by number, size, liver segment, and relationship to the main tumor. Distinguish liver-confined multifocal disease from regional nodal involvement and distant metastases.",
          "l": "Standard",
          "g": "D",
          "refs": [
            "capicca",
            "rcpafocality",
            "41172153"
          ],
          "pref": "Use the definitions in the “Multiple liver tumors” reference above. Confirm whether additional lesions are malignant when that uncertainty would change treatment.",
          "avoid": "Do not label all additional liver nodules as distant stage IV disease, assume satellites are harmless, or infer independent primary tumors from imaging alone.",
          "note": "The descriptions overlap biologically. Record imaging uncertainty and obtain expert radiology/pathology review rather than assigning a treatment solely from the label."
        }
      ],
      "alt": [
        {
          "t": "Plan molecular testing of a dedicated biliary specimen at the index ERCP where the disease presents as an indeterminate stricture rather than a mass and the alternative is a repeat procedure.",
          "l": "Reasonable",
          "g": "C",
          "refs": [
            "41905432",
            "30971436"
          ],
          "pref": "The patient entering the pathway as an indeterminate stricture, where pathology alone is weakest: in a 6-year prospective study of 2,116 patients across 28 institutions, pathologic assessment of ERCP brushings and biopsies had 44% sensitivity overall and 36% for intrahepatic or hilar strictures, while a DNA/RNA sequencing panel on separately collected specimens in a dedicated nucleic-acid buffer reached 82% sensitivity at 98% specificity and the combination 88% at 97%. Specificity was 99% for pathology, so sequencing bought sensitivity and gave up almost nothing.",
          "avoid": "Do not read a negative molecular result as excluding malignancy — in the original single-centre cohort there were 37 false negatives (25%) and the negative predictive value was only 63%, with sampling failure the usual explanation; in 12 of those cases the same panel found an alteration in the resected tumour. Only 2% of neoplastic strictures in the 2026 study were purely dysplastic, so outside primary sclerosing cholangitis this is earlier diagnosis of established cancer, not early detection, and no resectability or survival benefit has been shown. Payer authorisation and the dedicated collection buffer have to be arranged before the procedure, not after.",
          "note": "Correct the yield figure: therapeutically relevant alterations were reported in 20 of 150 cancers (13%) in the original single-centre cohort, and in the 2026 multi-institutional study in 137 of 458 cholangiocarcinomas (30%) — but only on the 161-gene version of the panel. The 28-gene version used in the original cohort did not detect FGFR2 fusions at all, which with chromatin-remodelling genes accounts for up to 20% of intrahepatic tumours, so a biliary specimen substitutes for the clinical decision 2 profile only if the panel actually run reports fusions. Downgraded from B: specimens were submitted at the endoscopist's discretion rather than consecutively, a stricture could be classified neoplastic on 12 months of clinical or radiographic progression rather than on tissue, and all testing was done in the laboratory that developed the assay."
        },
        {
          "t": "Add FDG-PET selectively, for suspected occult spread and for transplant staging.",
          "l": "Reasonable",
          "g": "B",
          "refs": [
            "nccn",
            "37770126",
            "37084797"
          ],
          "pref": "Where occult nodal or distant disease would change the operation, and in any patient being staged for a transplant protocol.",
          "avoid": "Do not substitute PET for MRI with MRCP in local planning; MRCP is preferred for biliary anatomy and ERCP or PTC are used more for therapeutic intervention.",
          "note": "BSG 2023 recommends FDG-PET-CT for nodal and distant disease as part of staging and EASL-ILCA recommends it routinely in apparently resectable patients, both more broadly than our selective wording — alignment worksheet, area 2. Read the strength of the broader recommendation honestly: the EASL-ILCA routine-PET statement passed its Delphi panel with only 78% agreement, the weakest consensus in that guideline's staging section, and AASLD 2023 states PET should not be used to assess the primary tumour."
        }
      ],
      "avoid": [
        {
          "t": "Do not place a biliary stent in a potentially resectable patient before the biliary-protocol imaging is complete and the drainage plan is agreed with the hepatobiliary surgeon.",
          "l": "Avoid",
          "g": "D",
          "refs": [
            "nccn",
            "37770126"
          ],
          "pref": "The only exception is cholangitis, which is drained immediately.",
          "avoid": "Stent-related inflammation obscures ductal extent, and drainage of the wrong side or an unnecessary procedure adds cholangitis risk and can delay both surgery and systemic therapy."
        },
        {

  "provenance": "Website language revised 23 October 2026 to use direct clinical questions and consistent terminology. The focality clarification additionally uses CAP intrahepatic bile-duct protocol v4.3 (June 2025), EASL–ILCA 2023 and current OPTN NLRB guidance. Wei 2025 (PMID 41172153) has since been read in full; it does not establish equivalence, operative superiority or an adopted staging change. Revised 7 October 2026 (Batch 08) after a full-text read of this page's reference depot: 37 structured abstracts, each carrying the authors' own stated limitations and an independent critique with its sources identified, against which every evidence string on this page was rechecked for the published number, for whether the critique undercuts what the string claims, and for whether the grade still follows. Thirty-three evidence strings changed. Three grades were lowered and the reason is recorded in each note: first-line chemo-immunotherapy in permanently unresectable liver-confined disease from A to B, because TOPAZ-1 and KEYNOTE-966 were 86% and 89% metastatic and say nothing about this population; offering adjuvant capecitabine from B to C, because BILCAP did not meet its intention-to-treat primary endpoint and only 19% of its patients had intrahepatic disease; and sequencing a dedicated biliary specimen at ERCP from B to C, because specimens were submitted non-consecutively, the reference standard allowed clinical and radiographic progression in place of tissue, and all testing was done in the laboratory that developed the assay. The transplant assessment was corrected most: the international explant series is now cited only for what it studied — 15 patients with single tumours of 2 cm or less, diagnosed on explant pathology, with mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma excluded and no requirement for disease stability on therapy — and the 3 cm ceiling and the six-month stability period in our criteria are attributed to EASL-ILCA, the OPTN review-board guidance and ILTS-ILCA rather than to that series. The ILTS-ILCA 2024 consensus is published twice and both records are cited (PMID 40014003, Liver Transplantation 2025; PMID 42312290, Liver Cancer 2026); the ESMO 2023 parent guideline (PMID 36372281) is now cited alongside its 2024 interim update, since the update covers only molecular diagnostics and advanced disease and leaves the surgical recommendations to the parent. Every reference the page cites was read in full. Still cited from the source document rather than from a full-text read: NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026, OPTN Policy 9 and the OPTN Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology guidance (December 2025), the Memorial Hermann roadmap and its alignment worksheet, and the HOPE4LIVER one-year histotripsy update, which in any case enrolled hepatocellular carcinoma and metastases rather than intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. Built from the Memorial Hermann Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma System Roadmap, Draft v0.6 (4 October 2026, including the 3 October 2026 liver-directed treatment revision), and its companion Guideline alignment worksheet of the same date, which compares the roadmap against AASLD 2023, OPTN 2025 review-board guidance, ESMO 2024 interim update, BSG 2023, LCSGJ 2022, ILTS-ILCA 2024 and NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026 across 16 areas. Evidence strings carry the published numbers and the published criticism; where the roadmap's label and the trial's primary endpoint diverge, both are stated and the local approval item is named. No recommendation was removed because its evidence turned out to be weak; the roadmap's position stands and the page now says how well supported it is. The liver-directed therapy matrix is read directly from the shared matrix file and is not reproduced here. This page reproduces a draft pending multidisciplinary approval: it is not active clinical policy, does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use. HAI sections updated 15 October 2026 to Batch 09. New studies were checked against indexed abstracts and the published ASCO abstract; new full-text PDFs remain to be acquired. No new full-text review is claimed for these additions."

No randomised evidence establishes a sequence among these options.","src":"Roadmap §3; FIGHT-202 PMID 38838500, FOENIX-CCA2 PMID 36652354, ClarIDHy PMID 34554208, ROAR PMID 32818466, HERIZON-BTC-01 PMID 41264278"},{"title":"Resectability, as the roadmap defines it","intro":"A surgical determination made by a hepatobiliary surgeon, not a radiological impression, reassessed whenever the disease or the liver changes.","rows":[["Hepatic extent","Favours: solitary or clustered disease clearable with an R0 margin and an adequate functional remnant. Against: multifocal disease across both lobes; additional malignant nodules that cannot all be safely resected."],["Vascular and biliary","Favours: inflow, outflow and biliary drainage preservable or reconstructable. Against: encasement precluding reconstruction; bilateral second-order biliary involvement."],["Nodal","Favours: no nodal disease, or regional nodes resectable within the standard basin — lymphadenectomy is part of the operation and informs adjuvant decisions. Against: nodal disease beyond the regional basin, including retroperitoneal or coeliac stations."],["Systemic","Favours: no extrahepatic disease. Against: any extrahepatic disease — this moves the pathway to systemic and molecularly directed therapy."],["Host","Favours: adequate reserve and performance status. Against: parenchymal disease or reserve that makes the necessary resection unsafe."]],"foot":"Three gaps to know about. 'Regional basin' is undefined in v0.6; AASLD 2023 draws the line at nodal metastasis beyond the hepatoduodenal and gastrohepatic ligaments. Numeric reserve rules remain specialty-approved local implementation, and the roadmap is silent on portal hypertension, which AASLD 2023 names a contraindication to resection. Where the tumour obstructs the biliary tree, the need for drainage, its route and its side are decided with the hepatobiliary surgeon before any non-emergency procedure — resection without preoperative drainage can be considered when the future remnant is large, and BSG 2023 puts that threshold at a remnant above 50%; cholangitis is drained without waiting.","src":"Roadmap §4; alignment worksheet areas 3, 4 and 6; NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026 p18"},{"title":"Transplant eligibility — the nonstandard MMaT-3 route","intro":"All of these are required by the described route, and our programme adds a protocol requirement on top.","rows":[["Diagnosis","Biopsy-proven solitary unresectable iCCA or mixed HCC-iCCA."],["Size","Tumour 3 cm or less."],["Liver","Underlying cirrhosis."],["Prior treatment","Locoregional or systemic therapy received."],["Stability period","Six months from diagnosis or last treatment with tumour stability: still 3 cm or less, no new lesions, no extrahepatic disease. Record both diagnosis and last-treatment dates and the serial scans that establish the interval — a response on one scan is insufficient."],["Extensions","Imaging every three months showing tumour still 3 cm or less with no extrahepatic disease; track the general 90-day extension cycle with a named renewal owner."],["Score and route","Nonstandard MMaT-3 exception: CCA diagnosis form plus a written narrative to the Adult Transplant Oncology Review Board. An MMaT-relative exception below 15 is assigned 15 (Policy 9.4.E)."],["Local restriction","A formally approved trial or prospective registry protocol, plus expert transplant-oncology selection. This is an additional institutional restriction, not an OPTN requirement."]],"foot":"MMaT is the median MELD at transplant for the donor hospital used in the match run, not one fixed national score, and the supplied document is review-board guidance, not OPTN policy or a clinical standard of care. Six months is also the period of radiographic stability the Houston Methodist–MD Anderson prospective series required before listing: 6 of 21 referred patients were transplanted, with 5-year survival 83.3% but recurrence-free survival 50% and a median cumulative tumour diameter of 14.2 cm. Poor differentiation is associated with worse outcome in the guidance footnote — a clinical selection concern, not a separately stated automatic exclusion. A local complete response is not an automatic transplant exception.","src":"Roadmap §8; OPTN Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology, December 2025, pp7–8; OPTN Policy 9.4.C–E, 9.5.A, 9.5.I; Lunsford PMID 29548617"},{"title":"BILCAP, as published","intro":"The trial the adjuvant capecitabine recommendation rests on. Not significant."],["Prespecified sensitivity analysis","Adjusted for nodal status, tumour grade and sex: hazard ratio 0.71 (95% CI 0.55–0.92), p=0.010."],["Per-protocol analysis","Hazard ratio 0.75 (95% CI 0.58–0.97), p=0.028. The trial was unmasked."],["Recurrence-free survival","24.4 versus 17.5 months, hazard ratio 0.75 over the first 24 months, with no difference from 24 to 60 months — the authors read this as deferred rather than prevented recurrence."],["Toxicity","Grade 3 or worse in 44% of the 213 treated, most often hand-foot syndrome (20%); 55% completed all eight cycles, 46% needed a dose reduction and 32% stopped for toxicity."],["The other adjuvant trials","ASCOT: 3-year survival 77.1% versus 67.6%, hazard ratio 0.69 — Japan only, S-1 unavailable in the United States, 13% intrahepatic. PRODIGE-12: negative for gemcitabine–oxaliplatin, grade 3–4 toxicity 73%. BCAT: no benefit for gemcitabine (hazard ratio 1.01) in extrahepatic bile duct cancer only, iCCA not eligible."]],"foot":"Local label: Reasonable consideration, grade B. NCCN Biliary Tract Cancers v1.2026 designates capecitabine preferred, category 1, while acknowledging the nonsignificant intention-to-treat analysis; AASLD 2023 and BSG 2023 treat it as standard, and LCSGJ 2022 makes a weak recommendation and reports no significant benefit in the intrahepatic subgroup. Lymphadenectomy was not mandated for intrahepatic patients, yet nodal status is one of the covariates that turns the sensitivity analysis positive. Offer capecitabine, discuss it with these numbers, and do not present it as settled — whether the label moves to Standard is unresolved approval item 3.","src":"BILCAP PMID 30922733; ASCOT PMID 36681415; PRODIGE-12 PMID 30707660; BCAT PMID 29405274; roadmap §7.1 and alignment worksheet area 11"},{"title":"Hepatic arterial infusion: selection, evidence and delivery","intro":"Reconciled with the current roadmap; clinical candidacy and transplant allocation remain separate decisions.","rows":[["Multicentre phase II evidence","PUMP-2, a three-centre nonrandomized phase II trial, enrolled 50 patients with unresectable liver-confined iCCA: 48 started HAI, partial response was 44%, disease control at six months 84%, and 5/50 (10%) underwent resection. Median OS was 22.3 months; three-year OS 31.5%. The historical comparator does not establish superiority over contemporary chemo-immunotherapy (PMID 41082695)."],["Mature pooled outcomes","The pooled individual-patient analysis of four phase II iCCA trials included 142 HAI-treated patients, with or without resectable regional nodes: median OS 26 months, five-year OS 15%, and 13/142 (9%) resected. Intention-to-treat five-year OS was 14%. This reuses constituent trial patients and must not be counted as independent replication or randomized comparative evidence (PMID 42331230)."],["Regional nodes and transplant separation","For iCCA HAI selection, distinguish resectable regional nodes from distant extrahepatic metastases. Selected regional nodal disease was permitted in prospective HAI evidence; distant spread is outside the proposed liver-confined HAI pathway. This allowance does not extend to transplant eligibility. Document nodal basin, resectability and separate LT assessment (PMIDs 31670750, 42331230)."],["Treatment position","Discuss HAI early for selected unresectable liver-confined iCCA at an experienced programme, with a systemic-treatment plan and a defined reassessment for resection. HAI, Y90 and ablative RT have no established head-to-head hierarchy. HAI is a control/conversion option, not proven standalone cure or a replacement for contemporary chemo-immunotherapy. Keep separate protocol-based transplant review and existing allocation requirements."],["Programme readiness","Before starting HAI, approve a named HPB surgeon with backup, medical oncologist, trained infusion nurses and pharmacy, nuclear-medicine perfusion assessment, IR rescue access, refill/maintenance coverage, liver-test monitoring and dose-hold rules, biliary-toxicity escalation and an outcomes registry. Reliable repeated visits are essential. Credentialing must cover the whole service, not pump implantation alone (PMIDs 39962001, 36346892)."],["Feasibility and medication safeguards","Avoid concurrent bevacizumab with HAI floxuridine because of increased biliary toxicity (PMID 24154839). Retain the broader no-concurrent-VEGF wording in the existing NCCN CRLM row. Assess hepatic reserve, portal hypertension/portal inflow, arterial anatomy, biliary obstruction or infection, prior liver radiation, operative fitness and reliable refill access. Age under 80 and lecture shunt cutoffs are centre practices, not universal evidence-based thresholds."]]}],"honest":[{"t":"Where the tumour obstructs the biliary tree, the need for drainage, its route and its side are decided with the hepatobiliary surgeon before any non-emergency procedure, particularly when a major hepatectomy is contemplated. Cholangitis is drained without waiting for that discussion.","why":"Standard, grade D. No comparative outcome data were identified for intrahepatic disease. The reasoning is mechanical rather than empirical: stent-related inflammation distorts the ductal extent that decides whether biliary resection and reconstruction are needed, and drainage of the wrong side adds cholangitis risk and delay.","refs":["nccn","37770126"]},{"t":"Exclude another primary before committing to this pathway, and record the entry dataset: tumour number and size, vascular and biliary involvement, regional nodal status, extrahepatic sites, ECOG, Child-Pugh and bilirubin, CA 19-9 and CEA, hepatitis serology.","why":"Both are grade D. The work-up justification is that metastatic adenocarcinoma can be histologically indistinguishable from intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and that treating a colorectal or pancreatic metastasis as iCCA is a recognised and consequential error — not that any study shows colonoscopy, age-appropriate breast imaging or a CK7/CK20/CDX2-type panel changes outcomes. The recorded dataset is a documentation standard the programme has chosen so that resectability, candidacy and the registry can be audited; no comparative outcome evidence supports the particular list. CA 19-9 and CEA are baseline and monitoring tests and never establish the diagnosis, and AASLD 2023 states explicitly that an elevated CA 19-9 alone must not be used to diagnose cholangiocarcinoma.","refs":["mhroadmap","37770126","36083140","35978598"]},{"t":"Match treatment to the alteration class reported, not to the gene name; other alterations in the same genes are not interchangeable and should be reviewed with a clinician experienced in molecular oncology before a matched agent is chosen.","why":"Standard, grade D. Locally reasonable and consistent with how the trials selected patients, but it is a consensus rule: no comparative data establish what happens when a non-canonical alteration is treated with a matched agent.","refs":["39864891","38838500","32203698"]},{"t":"Reassessment intervals: systemic therapy every 8–12 weeks by RECIST 1.1 with CA 19-9 as a supporting trend only; after resection every 3–6 months for 2 years then less frequently; after liver-directed therapy at 8–12 weeks allowing for the delayed response pattern; conversion intent at the pre-declared 2–3 month point, by formal surgical re-review rather than an imaging report alone.","why":"The response-assessment framework in this disease is expert consensus, not randomised evidence — grade C to D. NCCN states there are no data to support a specific surveillance schedule. Whether post-resection imaging should be fixed at 3-monthly, given that most recurrences are intrahepatic and some are re-resectable, or 6-monthly as most UK centres practise, is a local approval item (alignment worksheet, area 16).","refs":["nccn","37770126","31670746"]},{"t":"Biliary function is monitored alongside the disease: liver biochemistry at each assessment, and every patient with a biliary stent has a defined route for early detection of blockage. New jaundice, a rising bilirubin or cholangitis is evaluated promptly and does not wait for the next scheduled scan.","why":"Standard, grade D. Supported only indirectly — BSG 2023 attributes the better-than-expected survival of the ABC-06 active-symptom-control arm to proactive treatment of biliary obstruction and infection.","refs":["37770126","33798493"]},{"t":"The tumour board operating model, and the standing rule that trial eligibility is checked at diagnosis and at each progression.","why":"These are stakeholder-derived operating requirements, reproduced unchanged across every disease roadmap so the programme has one operating standard rather than five: submission form, triage, stable agenda, urgent referrals, required attendance, imaging reviewed rather than described, pathology pre-alerted, one recommendation with one owner and one reassessment date, documentation within one business day, registry closure. The trial-eligibility rule belongs to the same class. All are evidence grade D by construction — local policy choices with no comparative outcome evidence — and are labelled Standard because the programme has chosen them, not because trials support them. The eligibility rule is defensible in a disease where most of the molecularly matched evidence is single-arm, but no study shows that systematic eligibility checking improves outcome. Audit them for adherence, not for effectiveness.","refs":["mhroadmap"]},{"t":"Thresholds barring each liver-directed modality by liver function, and the order in which the modalities are listed.","why":"No comparative data define the cut-offs; they are safety conventions. The one hard stop that does come from data is cirrhosis before radioembolisation with chemotherapy, where hepatic failure occurred in 9 of 12 cirrhotic patients (75%), irreversible in 5, against 5 of 29 (17%) without cirrhosis, all reversible — and every irreversible case had whole-liver treatment. Everything else, including the liver-function limits for ablation and for ablative radiotherapy, is convention. Unresolved approval item 6, audited through decompensation after liver-directed therapy. The order itself carries no claim either. No randomised trial compares any two of hepatic arterial infusion, radioembolisation, chemoembolisation, ablative radiotherapy and thermal ablation in this disease, and none has been tested against a modern systemic backbone, so the sequence on the page reproduces the roadmap's table and the depth of each dataset rather than a hierarchy of evidence. Selection runs on treatment goal, target geometry, liver reserve and what the institution can deliver, and an upfront alternative chosen for anatomy or reserve is not a post-progression second line. Unresolved approval items 2, 6 and 7.","refs":["mhroadmap","31670746","26668346","31670750","21425151","34347159"]},{"t":"Retain the local requirement for a formally approved trial or prospective registry protocol and expert transplant-oncology selection before any transplantation for known intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.","why":"This is an additional institutional restriction, not an evidence finding. OPTN guidance describes six months of stability for its cirrhotic, unresectable, biopsy-proven solitary ≤3 cm route; ILTS–ILCA supports consideration after observation but sets no duration for that phenotype; the roadmap declines to open it outside a protocol because graft stewardship is an institutional judgement, not an evidence question. Unresolved approval item 5. What cannot honestly be given alongside it is an expected outcome. The published 5-year figures in iCCA span 25–73% overall survival and 29–82% recurrence-free survival, almost entirely from single-centre retrospective series, a range the ILTS-ILCA panel itself calls too wide to support a selection rule; almost every series describes iCCA found incidentally or misdiagnosed as hepatocellular carcinoma, so none is an intention-to-treat result and waitlist dropout for progression is unmeasured. A propensity-matched National Cancer Database comparison put transplant and resection within a few percentage points of each other at 5 years, and its authors argued resection should remain preferred for localised disease.","refs":["optnguid","42312290","40014003","36083140","37770126","34859465"]},{"t":"If intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is found in an explant removed for another indication, enter the patient into structured surveillance and the registry; immunosuppression minimisation and adjuvant therapy are individualised.","why":"Local policy. There is no comparative evidence for either immunosuppression minimisation or adjuvant therapy in this situation, and the published outcomes describe exactly this incidentally diagnosed population rather than a selected one.","refs":["27481548","34859465"]},{"t":"Mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma is out of scope for the hepatocellular carcinoma exception pathway: treat it as biliary disease for transplant purposes unless a protocol states otherwise, and flag it to the transplant team explicitly.","why":"Local policy, concordant with OPTN 2025, which routes mixed tumours through the same nonstandard request as iCCA, and with ILTS-ILCA 2024, which makes biopsy mandatory partly to exclude a mixed tumour. What is not known is how these patients do after transplantation. The index explant series excluded mixed tumours within a nodule outright and analysed the 33 explants with separate iCCA and hepatocellular nodules as a group outside its 48-patient study population, so it reports no outcome for them; the wider review literature notes that pooling mixed tumours with pure iCCA can make survival and recurrence look falsely favourable when the dominant phenotype is hepatocellular. The policy is therefore a precaution against an unquantified risk, not a reading of a dataset.","refs":["optnguid","42312290","27481548","34859465"]},{"t":"Adjuvant capecitabine after resection of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.","why":"BILCAP did not meet its primary endpoint. Intention-to-treat median overall survival was 51.1 versus 36.4 months with an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.81 (95% CI 0.63–1.04), p=0.097; significance appeared only in a prespecified sensitivity analysis adjusted for nodal status, grade and sex (0.71, 0.55–0.92) and in the per-protocol analysis (0.75, 0.58–0.97), in an unmasked trial whose analysis plan was not fully defined at the outset. Intrahepatic patients were 84 of 447 (19%) and the trial was not powered for site-specific effects, so no iCCA-specific benefit has been shown. The two guideline readings of that subgroup contradict each other — LCSGJ 2022 reports no significant benefit, EASL-ILCA cites a hazard ratio of 0.65 as the best of the subtypes — and they are not two datasets but two readings of one unpowered subgroup of a negative trial. What is actually known is that recurrence was deferred rather than prevented (no difference in recurrence-free survival from 24 to 60 months) and that 44% of treated patients had a grade 3 event, 32% stopped for toxicity and 55% finished all eight cycles. ACTICCA-1 has not reported. Our label is Reasonable consideration, grade C, and the conversation is the deliverable.","refs":["30922733","35978598","37084797","37770126","nccn"]},{"t":"The 3 cm tumour ceiling for a transplant referral.","why":"No study derived it. The series our page cites studied single tumours of 2 cm or less; EASL-ILCA concedes its own 3 cm figure is more permissive than the 2 cm cut-off used in the series and trials it cites, and ILTS-ILCA 2024 notes its ceiling mirrors the June 2024 OPTN review-board criteria rather than new data. Inside the index series the 2.1–3 cm band rests on 6 patients — single, not poorly differentiated tumours, 5-year survival 61%. A threshold nobody derived should be stated as a referral convention that the review board and the guidelines share, not as a size at which biology changes.","refs":["27481548","37084797","42312290","40014003","optnguid"]},{"t":"Six months from diagnosis or last treatment with tumour stability, as a transplant criterion.","why":"NLRB guidance itself specifies six months of stability for the solitary ≤3 cm cirrhotic iCCA/mixed-tumour exception route. ILTS–ILCA gives no duration for its small cirrhotic phenotype. Incidental explant series did not select on stability, while the prospective Houston programme selected locally advanced disease after at least six months of response or stability. These different populations do not establish that six months is the optimal biological interval.","refs":["27481548","29548617","42312290","40014003","optnguid"]},{"t":"First-line chemo-immunotherapy: the grade it carries in clinical decision 5, and the choice between the two agents.","why":"Graded B here rather than A, because the trials that establish the regimen did not study this population. TOPAZ-1 was 86% metastatic and KEYNOTE-966 89%, both ECOG 0–1, and the TOPAZ-1 investigators state that the trial says nothing about neoadjuvant, downstaging or peri-transplant use in liver-confined disease — which is exactly where the regimen is now borrowed. The absolute gains in the trials as run are 1.3 and 1.8 months of median survival, TOPAZ-1's proportional-hazards assumption was formally violated and it was reported at a prespecified interim analysis, and KEYNOTE-966 missed its prespecified boundaries for both progression-free survival and response. Grade A remains right for clinical decision 9. The choice between them is not an evidence finding either. There is no randomised comparison; ESMO declares the two interchangeable on an indirect comparison across trials differing in chemotherapy duration (gemcitabine capped at eight cycles in TOPAZ-1, continued to progression in KEYNOTE-966), geography and size, and states that no clinical, biochemical or molecular biomarker favours one. Neither trial found a predictive biomarker: benefit did not track PD-L1 in either, MSI status was missing for about half of TOPAZ-1 and only 10 KEYNOTE-966 patients were MSI-high. Present the choice as toxicity profile, schedule and access.","refs":["38319896","37075781","37084797","39864891"]},{"t":"The matched targeted agents in clinical decision 2, as a group.","why":"ClarIDHy and the subsequently reported first-line FIGHT-302 are randomized trials; neither demonstrated an ITT OS advantage. FIGHT-302 used GemCis rather than a modern chemo-immunotherapy comparator. ClarIDHy met progression-free survival (2.7 versus 1.4 months, hazard ratio 0.37) but final intention-to-treat survival was 10.3 versus 7.5 months, hazard ratio 0.79 (0.56–1.12), p=0.09, with 70% crossover; the crossover-adjusted HR is 0.49 with a corrected bootstrap 95% CI of 0.25–1.24 (October 2026; PMID 42879142), so adjusted OS is also not statistically significant. The initial pemigatinib, futibatinib, zanidatamab and dabrafenib–trametinib approvals rested on single-arm data, and none of those registration studies compared against second-line chemotherapy; first-line FIGHT-302 is a separate randomized update. The pemigatinib investigators explicitly warn against the cross-study comparison with pooled second-line chemotherapy that makes their agent look better, since FGFR2-fusion disease itself carries longer survival from diagnosis. Every one is industry-sponsored with sponsor involvement in design, analysis and writing. What is known is response rate and duration in a selected population; what is not known is survival against the alternative. A related choice sits on the same table: our rows require that HER2, NTRK and RET findings be captured but do not name trastuzumab deruxtecan, entrectinib, larotrectinib or selpercatinib, which ESMO 2024 recommends on level III grade A. The reason to hesitate is assay definition and evidence level rather than availability — ESMO concedes there are no standardised criteria for assessing HER2 status in biliary tract cancer and that no specific test can be recommended, while making two HER2-directed recommendations that depend on that undefined assay, and zanidatamab's own data are reported for biliary tract cancer as a whole with no breakdown by subsite. Alignment worksheet, area 14.","refs":["34554208","32416072","38838500","36652354","41264278","32818466","39864891"]},{"t":"Hepatic arterial infusion as the strongest regional option.","why":"The earlier phase 2 study included 38 treated patients at one institution, selected from 84 screened, with the comparison drawn from historical systemic series; the linked editorial judged the case for locoregional therapy in unresectable cholangiocarcinoma still unsettled without a randomised trial, and the authors themselves called for one. The retrospective comparison that gives 30.8 versus 18.4 months had all HAI patients surgically staged against 42% of a 26-patient comparator of whom only 30% received gemcitabine–cisplatin, so stage migration favours HAI; 44 of its 93 HAI patients came from earlier phase 2 trials, and it reports no pump complication or biliary toxicity rate at all. Conversion to curative-intent resection occurred in 8 of 236 patients (3%). Delivery is harder than the figures suggest: 71% received the expected floxuridine dose over the first 3 months and 47% over the next 6, and grade 4 pump or arterial complications forced withdrawal in 11% of the lead-centre cohort and 30% of the 10-patient confirmatory cohort. The deciding variables for the programme are pump expertise, nursing infrastructure and case volume, not the evidence. Updated evidence: PUMP-2 (PMID 41082695), a three-centre nonrandomized phase II study: 50 pumps placed, 48 patients started HAI, partial response 44%, six-month disease control 84%, resection 5/50 (10%), median OS 22.3 months and three-year OS 31.5%. The 2026 pooled analysis of four phase II trials (PMID 42331230) reports 142 treated patients, median OS 26 months, five-year OS 15% (ITT 14%), and 13/142 resections (9%). The pooled cohorts overlap the constituent trials; these are not independent replications or randomized comparisons with modern chemo-immunotherapy.","refs":["31670750","26695839","nccn"]},{"t":"Y90 radioembolisation as a conversion strategy.","why":"One single-arm phase 2 of 41 patients, run only at centres experienced with glass microspheres and part-funded by the microsphere manufacturer, with several authors as its consultants. Its 22% downstaging and 20% R0 rates describe a doubly selected cohort: 4 of 45 patients were excluded at the planning angiogram and 9 of 41 had major protocol deviations, leaving 32 per protocol. The authors state tumour-absorbed dose rather than a generic liver dose probably drives outcome, so the regimen does not transfer as written, and grade 3–4 toxicity affected 71%. Two patients whose disease stayed unresectable but controlled were offered transplant and both recurred, at 16 and 17 months. The confirmatory randomised SIRCCA trial has not reported.","refs":["31670746","nccn"]},{"t":"Ablative radiotherapy doses, and the 80.5 Gy figure.","why":"It is an association in a retrospective single-centre series of 79 patients in which only 19 received the high dose. Those 19 also had significantly smaller planning target volumes (median 415 versus 614 cm³, p=0.02), and the high doses arrived with breath-hold gating and daily diagnostic-quality CT image guidance after 2010, so anatomy, technique and era are all confounded with dose — patients treated after 2010 survived 50 versus 24 months. The prospective proton data are a safety and local-control signal, not a survival finding: the 39-patient iCCA cohort had no prespecified efficacy hypothesis, median delivered dose was 58.0 GyE against an intended 67.5, every local failure occurred below 60 GyE, local failures kept accruing past 2 years and 53.8% developed distant metastases. The randomised answer was deferred to NRG GI-001, which closed early for poor accrual. Treat the dose as a planning aspiration, not a threshold.","refs":["26503201","26668346"]},{"t":"Thermal ablation as an alternative to resection for a small tumour.","why":"The cohort that reports parity did not test our rule. Its entry criterion was Milan-equivalent — a single tumour up to 5 cm, or up to three each 3 cm or less — not the under-3 cm wording the page uses, and within it a 3–5 cm tumour was an independent risk factor for disease-free survival after ablation but not after resection. The equivalence headline comes from a post hoc split at 2017, where the later comparison was underpowered (p=0.129), and a nonsignificant difference is not equivalence; margin was measured by post-ablation CT or MR in one arm and on the specimen in the other, which the authors accept may bias the mediation result their conclusion rests on. Resection still outperformed ablation in patients under 60, with hepatolithiasis, with left-lobe tumours and with GGT above 50 U/L. The pooled meta-analysis behind the under-3 cm limit is 20 retrospective studies with I² up to 85%, publication bias on 3-year survival (Egger p=0.039), a dichotomised size variable and no individual patient data; pooled recurrence-free survival was 40.0% at 1 year and 19.2% at 3. The structural problem for a surgeon is different: ablation yields no specimen and no nodal dissection, so there is no pathological node status to drive the clinical decision 8 decision, and node-negativity rests on imaging whose sensitivity for nodal metastasis is 20–61%.","refs":["38261915","34347159","41528222","37084797","nccn"]},{"t":"Routine regional lymphadenectomy at every iCCA resection.","why":"No guideline recommends it on evidence of survival benefit. LCSGJ 2022 makes no recommendation on node dissection at all and warns that prophylactic dissection in cirrhosis increases complications; ESMO 2023 recommends routine hepatoduodenal-ligament dissection on level IV evidence; BSG 2023 says nothing about extent or node yield, which its own critics identify as a gap given that the adjuvant recommendation it then makes turns on nodal status; AASLD 2023 likewise makes no statement. Keeping it in every operation is a staging decision the programme has made so that the adjuvant conversation and the registry have a denominator, not a survival finding. Unresolved; audit the node yield, not the outcome.","refs":["35978598","36372281","37770126","36083140"]},{"t":"Two resectability criteria this page states but does not define: the regional nodal basin, and the liver-reserve limit.","why":"The basin is not defined in this version. AASLD 2023 draws the boundary at nodal metastasis beyond the hepatoduodenal and gastrohepatic ligaments and NCCN at beyond the porta hepatis; an undefined basin cannot be audited and two surgeons can reach opposite conclusions on the same scan. Clinical nodal staging is also insensitive here — reported sensitivity for nodal metastasis is 20–61% — so the criterion is applied to an uncertain input. On the other side the roadmap is silent on portal hypertension, while AASLD 2023 names decompensated cirrhosis and portal hypertension as contraindications to resection and LCSGJ 2022 builds its whole algorithm on Child-Pugh class, sending Child-Pugh C to palliative care. No comparative data define numeric reserve thresholds in iCCA, so any local rule is a safety convention, which is why it stays specialty-approved local implementation rather than being asserted here. Alignment worksheet, areas 3 and 4.","refs":["36083140","nccn","35978598","38261915"]},{"t":"Conversion therapy with a declared reassessment, and the rates quoted for it.","why":"The 36.4% and 53% conversion rates are retrospective Japanese series quoted by LCSGJ 2022, which in the same document records no evidence of benefit for neoadjuvant chemotherapy and makes no recommendation; the denominators are not defined and those series report median survival of 24.1 months in converted patients against 25.7 months in those primarily resectable. AASLD 2023 states the role of neoadjuvant downstaging is not well defined and BSG 2023 does not recommend routine neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Neither modern chemo-immunotherapy trial supports downstaging, since both were almost entirely metastatic. The prospective conversion numbers that do exist are small: 9 of 41 downstaged and 8 resected with Y90 plus chemotherapy, 4 of 38 with hepatic arterial infusion. What is defensible is the discipline — record the obstacle to R0, declare the reassessment date, hold a formal surgical re-review — not a conversion rate.","refs":["35978598","36083140","37770126","31670746","31670750"]},{"t":"Ordering broad molecular profiling at diagnosis rather than at progression.","why":"The argument is operational, not biological, and no study shows that ordering earlier improves outcome. What supports it is turnaround of two to four weeks against a second-line decision that cannot wait, plus the screening arithmetic: 783 patients screened to enrol 103 in FOENIX-CCA2, 1,206 prescreened to find 107 fusion-positive patients for FIGHT-202, and a BRAF V600E yield reported at 9% but nearer 5–7% in practice because sites entered known positives. Our grade B is lower than ESMO's level I grade A and BSG's strong recommendation on high-quality evidence; the obstacle in practice is payer authorisation and ordering discipline, which is why this is audited as a proportion rather than asserted as a standard. The plasma alternative is weaker than its headline figure suggests: the 87% quoted for plasma detection of an FGFR2 fusion comes from 83 of 95 FOENIX-CCA2 patients already known to be tissue-positive, so it measures concordance in a positive population, not the chance of finding a target de novo. Evidence strings carry the published numbers and the published criticism; where the roadmap's label and the trial's primary endpoint diverge, both are stated and the local approval item is named.
